title: Triggering and Skipping Workflows Safely
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of triggering and skipping workflows safely and identify when it should be used.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on triggering and skipping workflows safely. Avoid privileged workflows that execute untrusted pull-request content; understand which events the repository token can trigger and whether the workflow should run at all. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Triggering and Skipping Workflows Safely matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Avoid privileged workflows that execute untrusted pull-request content; understand which events the repository token can trigger and whether the workflow should run at all. Choose triggers deliberately. Event type, branch/tag filters, path filters, activity types, and token-trigger behavior determine when automation runs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Avoid privileged workflows that execute untrusted pull-request content; understand which events the repository token can trigger and whether the workflow should run at all. Choose triggers deliberately. Event type, branch/tag filters, path filters, activity types, and token-trigger behavior determine when automation runs. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Conditional triggering
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Avoiding unintended recursive runs
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Workflow-triggering rules for GITHUB_TOKEN
items.text: Declare only the token scopes the job requires. A read-only job should not receive write access; verify permissions at workflow and job scope and review organization policy.

items.text: For comparing pull_request and pull_request_target, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. name: Validate workflow configuration

  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:

      - run: echo "Replace with a real validation command"

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain triggering and skipping workflows safely, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Choose triggers and filters that run the right validation at the right time without exposing privileged jobs.

content.task: Apply triggering and skipping workflows safely to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Avoid privileged workflows that execute untrusted pull-request content; understand which events the repository token can trigger and whether the workflow should run at all. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.

Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
